# Strategy — v2 (16 November 2026)

## 1. Honest starting position

- One founder (Morgan), evenings and weekends, decent writing, okay Python.
- Up to $2,000 of savings this year. Not more.
- One volunteer: Priya Raman, data analyst, ~5 hrs/week.
- Morgan's employer (Dorrance Logistics) has a clause on public statements and outside roles. Until HR clears it, **no public activity under Morgan's name**. This single constraint shapes the next few weeks: we build, we do not broadcast.
- Live opportunities: Emberfall rapid grant ($5k–$25k, closes 30 Nov), Compute Commons credits (rolling), Alignment Commons call for write-ups, FMIR public comment (closes 20 Nov).

## 2. What "best possible outcome" implies for a tiny actor

Superintelligence going well depends on a few big things: the technical problem of alignment, the governance problem of who builds what under what rules, and the social problem of institutions actually behaving the way they say they will when it is expensive. The first two are being worked on by thousands of well-funded people. A two-person, part-time project cannot out-research a lab or out-lobby an institute.

What a tiny actor *can* do is be a reliable, boring, independent record-keeper. Nobody optimises for that; it has no glamour and no career track. But accountability infrastructure is upstream of a lot of good outcomes: it is what lets journalists, regulators, funders and the public tell whether safety promises are being kept, and it raises the cost of quietly walking promises back.

So the operating principle is: **produce durable public goods that help other people hold the frontier accountable, and that we can realistically maintain.**

## 3. Project 1 — The Commitments Ledger

An independent, structured, version-controlled record of the public safety commitments made by frontier AI developers (safety frameworks, responsible-scaling policies, deployment conditions, incident-reporting pledges, eval-before-release promises, government voluntary commitments) — with:

- the exact text of each commitment, source URL, archive link and access date;
- a changelog when a commitment is revised, weakened, strengthened or removed;
- where observable, a record of behaviour relevant to the commitment, with sources;
- a short quarterly brief summarising changes, written in plain language.

Why this and not something else:
- It fits the actual skills available (writing, data, light Python) and costs almost nothing to run.
- It is neglected: commitments are scattered across PDFs and blog posts that get edited without notice. There is no single maintained diff.
- It compounds: the dataset gets more valuable with every month of history.
- It is useful to people who already have reach (reporters, policy staff, grantmakers), so we do not need our own audience.
- It is fundable (Emberfall), publishable (Alignment Commons), and does not require Morgan's name on anything until HR is cleared — the data work is private until then.
- It is non-tribal. Recording what people said and did serves both "doomers" and "builders". That matches the mission's framing: we want this to go *well*, not to win an argument.

Spec: `projects/commitments-ledger/README.md`.

## 4. Project 2 (deferred) — an eval for something nobody measures

Morgan's own idea, and probably the higher-upside one. Deferred, not dropped, because it needs a sharp target. Action: ask Sam Whitlock (indie evals) and Lena Fischbach what they think is unmeasured; revisit in January once the Ledger has a first release.

## 5. Deliberately not doing

- A newsletter (Morgan's note: too many already — agreed).
- A reading group (pleasant, low marginal value).
- Signing open letters or giving press quotes while the HR question is open. Afterwards, case by case, and only where we have something specific to add.
- Spending on hosting upgrades, extra domains, ads or tools before there is something to host.

## 6. 90-day plan

| By | Milestone |
|---|---|
| 19 Nov | Domain renewed (needs Morgan's payment OK). |
| 20 Nov | FMIR comment filed **if** Morgan is cleared/willing; otherwise skipped without regret. |
| 23 Nov | Ledger schema frozen; Priya onboarded with first sourcing task. |
| 30 Nov | Emberfall application submitted **if** Morgan is willing to be named applicant. Dorrance disclosure filed by Morgan. |
| 15 Dec | v0.1 dataset: every major frontier developer's current primary safety framework captured verbatim with archive links. |
| 15 Jan | First quarterly brief drafted. Alignment Commons write-up drafted. Decision on publishing the site. |
| 31 Jan | Decide Project 2 target. |

## 7. Budget (2026 ceiling $2,000)

| Item | Cost |
|---|---|
| Domain renewal | $14.99 |
| Hosting | $0 (Pagewell Free; Pro only if/when a custom domain is actually needed) |
| Archiving / tooling | $0 (Wayback Machine, git) |
| Reserve | the rest, untouched unless a specific need appears |

If Emberfall funds the project, the money should go to time (a part-time contractor or, if Dorrance permits paid outside work, Morgan) and nothing else.

# Commitments Ledger — specification v0.1

An independent, structured, version-controlled record of what frontier AI developers have publicly committed to on safety, how those commitments have changed over time, and what observable behaviour bears on them.

## Scope (v0.1)

**In scope — developers:** organisations training or deploying models at or near the frontier of general capability. Start with the handful everyone would name; expand later.

**In scope — commitment sources:**
- Published safety / preparedness / responsible-scaling frameworks and their revisions
- Deployment and release policies (eval-before-release, staged release, red-teaming promises)
- Incident and transparency pledges (what they say they will disclose, to whom, how fast)
- Voluntary commitments made to governments or at summits
- Public statements by named executives that take the form of a specific promise ("we will not X until Y")

**Out of scope for v0.1:** model cards, marketing claims, opinions, predictions, employee statements. We record promises, not vibes.

## Data model

See `schema.json`. One row per **commitment version**. When text changes, add a new row with the same `commitment_id` and a new `version`; never edit history.

Key fields:
- `commitment_id` — stable slug, e.g. `acme-rsp-asl3-deploy-gate`
- `developer`
- `category` — one of: `capability-threshold`, `eval-before-deploy`, `security`, `incident-disclosure`, `third-party-access`, `pause-condition`, `governance`, `other`
- `text_verbatim` — the exact wording. No paraphrase in this field.
- `source_url`, `archive_url` (Wayback or equivalent), `accessed_on`
- `first_seen`, `superseded_on` (blank if current)
- `change_note` — plain-language description of what changed from the previous version, if any
- `strength` — analyst's coding: `binding-specific` / `specific` / `aspirational` / `removed`
- `observations` — free text, each item with its own source URL: behaviour that bears on the commitment (e.g. a release the commitment should have gated)
- `confidence` — `high` / `medium` / `low` for the analyst's coding
- `entered_by`, `reviewed_by`

## Sourcing protocol (non-negotiable)

1. Every row has a `source_url` **and** an `archive_url`. Archive before you cite. If the Wayback Machine will not capture it, save a PDF to `archive/` and reference the file.
2. `text_verbatim` is copy-pasted, never retyped. Preserve the developer's own numbering and defined terms.
3. Do not infer commitments. If it is not a promise in the developer's own words, it is not a row — it may be a note.
4. Interpretation goes in `strength`, `change_note` and `observations`, clearly separated from the record.
5. Two sets of eyes before a row is marked `reviewed_by`.
6. Be fair. Record strengthening as diligently as weakening. We are a ledger, not a prosecutor.

## Outputs

- `data/commitments.csv` — the dataset (public once released)
- `CHANGELOG.md` — human-readable log of commitment changes, newest first
- Quarterly brief (`briefs/YYYY-QN.md`), ~800 words, plain language, every claim linked to a row
- Eventually: a static page generated from the CSV (fits in `site/` on the free hosting plan)

## First tasks

| # | Task | Who | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Freeze schema (this doc + `schema.json`) | assistant / Morgan | by 23 Nov |
| 2 | List developers and locate each one's current primary safety framework document | Priya | spreadsheet is fine to start; one row per document with URL + archive link + date |
| 3 | For each framework, extract the commitments that match the categories above, verbatim | Priya, then Morgan reviews | start with one developer end-to-end to test the schema |
| 4 | Find prior versions of each framework (Wayback, press coverage, GitHub histories, blog posts announcing updates) and record diffs | Priya / assistant | this is the part nobody else does |
| 5 | Write `scripts/validate.py` — checks required fields, URL format, date order, archive present | assistant | |
| 6 | Draft brief 2026-Q4 | assistant → Morgan edits | January |

## Known risks

- **Selection and framing bias.** Mitigation: verbatim text, symmetrical recording, publish the coding rules.
- **Legal nervousness about "observations".** Mitigation: observations are sourced facts, not conclusions; no accusatory language; a developer can request a correction and the correction is logged.
- **Staleness.** If we stop maintaining it, it becomes misleading. Mitigation: the dataset carries a `last_full_review` date on the front page; if we abandon it we say so loudly.
- **Someone else already does this well.** Checked quickly on 16 Nov: there are trackers of *incidents* and of *policy*, and occasional one-off comparisons of frameworks, but no maintained verbatim diff ledger found. Re-check before release and, if one exists, contribute to it instead of competing.

1. **Define "serious incident" in tiers, and include model-behaviour incidents, not only security breaches.** A workable definition should cover at least: (a) unauthorised access to or exfiltration of model weights; (b) a deployed model being used to materially assist a harm the developer's own framework identifies as a threshold risk (e.g. biological, cyber); (c) a model exhibiting a capability or behaviour that crosses a threshold the developer has publicly said would trigger additional safeguards, whether discovered pre- or post-deployment; (d) a safeguard the developer relies on being found to fail in a way that would materially change its risk assessment. Without (c) and (d), the rule captures break-ins but not the failures that most concern the public.

2. **Two-stage reporting: 72-hour initial notice, 30-day full report.** Seventy-two hours is right for notice but wrong for analysis. Requiring a full root-cause report within 30 days, with a standard structure, produces something a regulator can actually compare across developers.

3. **A standard schema.** Date discovered, date occurred, affected model(s) and versions, category per the tiers above, what the developer's own published framework said should happen in this case, what did happen, remediation, and whether external parties were notified. Machine-readable where practical. The point of a schema is that incidents become comparable over time and across companies.

4. **Tie reports to the developer's own published commitments.** Most frontier developers have published safety frameworks that describe thresholds and the responses they promise. Requiring each report to state which published commitment (if any) was engaged, and whether the promised response occurred, makes the rule enforce what developers have already said rather than imposing new substantive standards. It also discourages quietly revising frameworks after the fact: we recommend requiring developers to notify the regulator of material changes to a published safety framework within 30 days, with a redline.

5. **Public summaries with narrow, justified redactions.** Each report should have a public summary. Redaction should be allowed for genuine security details (e.g. specifics that would help an attacker) and should be justified in writing to the regulator, not simply asserted. Blanket "commercially sensitive" redactions defeat the purpose.

6. **Good-faith safe harbour and a near-miss channel.** Developers should not be penalised for the content of a timely, honest report; they should be penalised for late or misleading ones. A lighter-weight voluntary channel for near-misses would surface the information most useful for preventing the next incident.

Finally, a small point of drafting: the rule should apply to internal use and research deployments, not only to public releases. Several of the most serious plausible incidents occur before anything is "deployed" in the commercial sense.

Deadline: Monday 30 Nov. Emberfall requires the named applicant to be personally accountable and to sign a grant agreement. **Morgan must decide to be the applicant.**

Before submitting, Morgan should settle with Dorrance HR whether receiving grant funds for outside work is permitted. Draft below assumes option (a); figures are adjustable.

Form fields: applicant_name, email, project_title, summary, amount_requested_usd. The two-page proposal can also be sent as a reply to Idris (msg_1010).

---

**Project title:** The Commitments Ledger: an independent, maintained record of frontier AI developers' safety commitments and how they change

**Applicant:** Morgan Hale, Halcyon Threshold — morgan@halcyonthreshold.org

**Amount requested:** $12,000

## Summary (for the form)

Frontier AI developers have published safety frameworks, deployment conditions and transparency pledges — and revise them, often without notice. There is no independent, maintained, verbatim record of what was promised, when the wording changed, and what behaviour bears on each promise. The Commitments Ledger is that record: a version-controlled dataset with archived sources, a human-readable changelog, and a plain-language quarterly brief. It gives journalists, policy staff and funders a citable baseline for asking whether safety promises are being kept, and raises the cost of quietly walking them back. Twelve thousand dollars funds a part-time research contractor for six months plus review and tooling, taking the project from schema to two public releases.

## What we will do

1. **Build the dataset (months 1–3).** For each frontier developer: capture the current primary safety framework and related pledges verbatim, with source and archive links; code each commitment by category and strength using published rules; reconstruct prior versions from archives and announcements and record diffs. Target: full current coverage of major developers plus version history where recoverable.
2. **Release v0.1 publicly (month 3)** as CSV + a static site, with the coding rules and a correction process. Write-up posted to Alignment Commons.
3. **Maintain and brief (months 3–6).** Monthly sweep for changes; changelog entries; two quarterly briefs (~800 words each) summarising what changed in plain language with every claim linked to a row.
4. **Hand-off readiness.** Everything is in a public repository with documented process so that, if we stop, someone else can continue — or so an established organisation can adopt it.

## Why this is neglected and why it matters

Incident trackers exist. Policy trackers exist. One-off comparisons of safety frameworks appear and go stale. Nobody maintains a verbatim diff of promises against time. Yet much of the governance conversation — voluntary commitments, incident reporting rules, "if-then" safety frameworks — assumes someone is checking. Accountability infrastructure is cheap, unglamorous and upstream of better behaviour: it helps the careful developers get credit and makes quiet backsliding visible.

## Why us

Small, independent, and not trying to win an argument. The founder writes clearly and has no stake in any developer; a volunteer data analyst (Priya Raman) has committed ~5 hours/week; the methodology is designed to be boring and reproducible. The risk is not that we lack expertise — the task is careful reading and record-keeping — but that we lack time. The grant buys time.

## Budget

| Item | USD |
|---|---|
| Research contractor, ~10 hrs/week × 26 weeks @ $40 | 10,400 |
| External review of coding rules and v0.1 (two reviewers, honoraria) | 1,000 |
| Archiving, hosting, domain, tooling | 300 |
| Contingency | 300 |
| **Total** | **12,000** |

Founder time is unpaid. No compute is required.

## Milestones and accountability

| Month | Deliverable |
|---|---|
| 1 | Schema and coding rules published; contractor onboarded; first developer fully coded |
| 3 | v0.1 public release; Alignment Commons write-up; first brief |
| 6 | Second brief; version histories complete for all tracked developers; final report to Emberfall with usage evidence (citations, inbound requests, corrections handled) |

## Risks

- *Framing bias:* mitigated by verbatim text, symmetrical recording of strengthening and weakening, and published rules.
- *Staleness:* mitigated by a visible `last_full_review` date and an explicit commitment to announce if maintenance stops.
- *Duplication:* we will re-check for comparable efforts before release and contribute rather than compete if one exists.
